name: Delphinium
lede: Delphinium is a color named for the tall blue garden flower, a name that the chart-makers kept even after the swatch grew greyer than the petals.

sections.title: A flower's blue
sections.body:
Paterson defines *delphinium blue* as a blue tinged with violet, and he adds that *delphinium* alone is also used [1]. He lists *delphine* as a shade possibly the same, and *Devonshire blue* as a paler delphinium blue [1]. All of these sit in his blue family [1].

The poet and filmmaker Derek Jarman used the flower in *Chroma*, his book on color, which has a blue poem with the line "delphinium days" and, in a later poem, a blue delphinium placed on a grave [2]. In Baty's survey of historical color charts, the petals of the plant also are the plate's example of pitch, or brownish black [3]. The flower, then, runs from violet-blue to near-black.

sections.title: The swatch is greyer than the flower
sections.body: This swatch comes from Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color* of 1930, as cited in the ISCC-NBS circular of 1955 [4]. The system calls the nearest region a grayish blue, 4.0 CIEDE2000 units away [4]. It is a muted slate blue, with a lightness of 47 and chroma of only 15 [4]. Its hue leans slightly toward violet, which matches Paterson's description, but Paterson's blue tinged with violet suggests a stronger color than this low-chroma swatch [1][4]. Close neighbors are [[steel-blue]], [[blue-grey]] and [[periwinkle]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch is a common muted blue in paint. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 212 works [5]. It is most often a quiet mid-tone, and in 22 per cent of cases a highlight [5]. Claude Monet is its most devoted user in the within-painting lens, in 4 of 50 of his works here, about five times the baseline, though that is a small n [5]. The twentieth century shows 2.3 times the expected rate [5]. As always these are photographs of varnished paintings, not pigment tests [5].
